Program:

int day = 2;
switch (day) {
    case 1: System.out.println("Mon");
    case 2: System.out.println("Tue");
    case 3: System.out.println("Wed");
    default: System.out.println("Other");
}

Question: What does this program print, and why?

Student's answer: It prints only Tue. day is 2, so the switch jumps to case 2, prints Tue, and then the switch is finished. The other cases are skipped because they do not match. Settings: width 3, depth 3, prune llm, backend claude-cli, model claude-opus-5-5

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | mis:control_flow->CodeAfterIfSkipped | wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. | right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way. | | mis:control_flow->FalseConditionRestartsProgram | wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. | right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement. | | mis:control_flow->FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode | wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. | right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:control_flow->IfConditionWatched | wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). | right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch. | | mis:control_flow->IfWaitsForCondition | wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. | right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it. | | mis:control_flow->LoopImpliedByOneTest | wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. | right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop. | | mis:control_flow->NoShortCircuit | wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them) | right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramEndsAfterLoop | wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. | right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop. | | mis:control_flow->ProgramLooksAhead | wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. | right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them. | | mis:control_flow->ReturnDoesNotExitLoop | wrong rule: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values. | right rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass. | | mis:control_flow->StatementsRunInAnyOrder | wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. | right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom. |

println, misconceptions: 6 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:println->PrintWithoutFinalNewline | wrong rule: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away. | right rule: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed. | | mis:println->IdentifierCaseInsensitive | wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. | right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names. | | mis:println->ParenthesesOnlyIfArgument | wrong rule: println with nothing to print can be written System.out.println; without the parentheses. | right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();. | | mis:println->PrintEqualsPrintln | wrong rule: print and println do the same thing, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on separate lines. | right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line. | | mis:println->PrintNewLineFirst | wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. | right rule: println(s) prints s and then the newline. | | mis:println->PrintedTextIsExecuted | wrong rule: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code). | right rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x. |

switch_statement, level ways: 16 edges offered

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | lvl:switch_statement@L0#0 | level L0 way everyday_reading: Folk meaning: everyday 'switch' means flip to one setting, and 'case' reads like 'in case of X do Y', a self-contained rule. Novices therefore expect only the matching case to run. In a Java switch statement, the case labels are only entry points: execution starts at the matching label and falls through the following cases until a break. | | lvl:switch_statement@L0#2 | level L0 way inconsistent_trace: Applies the LT rule unevenly: on a trace the selector is matched correctly but execution stops at the next case label on some runs and falls through on others, or default is run even though a case matched. (here mixing in: "After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break") | | lvl:switch_statement@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: Selection statement: switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... } chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression. | | lvl:switch_statement@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches. | | lvl:switch_statement@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace. | | lvl:switch_statement@L2#1 | level L2 way output_prediction: A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with day = 3, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat. | | lvl:switch_statement@L2#2 | level L2 way one_step_execution: One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change. | | lvl:switch_statement@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is expr == constant on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (income < 47450) must stay an if-else chain. | | lvl:switch_statement@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop. | | lvl:switch_statement@L3#2 | level L3 way purpose_of_the_whole: Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (case "apple": case "banana":) map several values to one action. | | lvl:switch_statement@L4#0 | level L4 way predict_a_change: When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label. | | lvl:switch_statement@L4#1 | level L4 way transfer_to_a_new_program: Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value. | | lvl:switch_statement@L4#2 | level L4 way diagnose_an_error: rule broken: Without break, execution falls through into the following cases.
